outcome: In August 2026, Huang, Jackson, Lee, Poonen, Pries and Zhang gave an explicit degree-23 polynomial over Q whose splitting field has Galois group the Mathieu group M23, completing the realization of all 26 sporadic simple groups as Galois groups over Q; the general inverse Galois problem (every finite group) remains open, and the authors' own acknowledgements describe substantial AI assistance in the research process, though not in producing the mathematical text or final verification.

ai.basis_quote: No text in this article was written by AI. We used Claude Fable 5, Claude Opus 4.8, and ChatGPT 5.6 Sol for searching the literature, code generation, testing hypotheses, ruling out other approaches, devising computational strategies, checking our results, and proofreading our manuscript. ... Our final results were verified in Magma and PARI/GP without the use of AI.
ai.disclosed_cost: Anthropic provided each author a 3-month Claude Max subscription (no token/compute figures disclosed)

disputes.summary: Sources disagree on how central AI was to the mathematics. The paper's own acknowledgements list AI uses that read as auxiliary (literature search, code generation, hypothesis testing, ruling out approaches, computational strategy, checking, proofreading) and explicitly say no article text was AI-written and final verification was AI-free. A co-authored blog post ('Where to Point the Telescope', Proofs and Prompts) and Scientific American's coverage describe AI more substantively — 'multi-agent AI workflows... generate and test code, analyze data, ... organize large computations, and monitor and recover from failures', and AI 'numerically approximating' the Belyi map equations, with a human insight about switching coordinate systems (cutting required precision from 90 to 40 digits) being the decisive step. Epoch AI's FrontierMath Open Problems page went further, introducing a new 'human + AI' solved-status label specifically because 'comments from the authors make it clear that AI was instrumental in solving this problem' -- a stronger characterization than the paper's own wording of 'devising computational strategies'.

summary: The general inverse Galois problem (is every finite group a Galois group over Q?) remains fully open. What happened in the window is a case: an August 2026 preprint (arXiv:2608.08538, MIT mirror at math.mit.edu/~poonen/papers/M23.pdf) by Huang, Jackson, Lee, Poonen, Pries and Zhang exhibits an explicit degree-23 polynomial with rational coefficients whose splitting field over Q has Galois group the Mathieu group M23, the last of the 26 sporadic finite simple groups to be realized (the other 25 were done 1984-1989). This is squarely a §3.1 'case' -- it removes one specific finite group from the territory of the open problem without touching the problem as stated -- so status is partial, direction confirmed (the group is realized, as the inverse Galois heuristic expects). The AI question is the interesting part. The paper's own acknowledgements are explicit and are the primary basis for ai_role: they used Claude Fable 5, Claude Opus 4.8 and ChatGPT 5.6 Sol for literature search, code generation, hypothesis testing, ruling out approaches, devising computational strategies, checking results and proofreading, while stating plainly that no article text was AI-written and the final verification (in Magma and PARI/GP) was AI-free. Under the rubric's test -- 'what did the model produce that appears in the final result?' -- 'devising computational strategies' and 'testing hypotheses' sit right at the assisted/none boundary: they are more than pure checking or proofreading, since they describe the AI contributing to how the search for the polynomial/Belyi map was carried out, which is part of the mathematical route to the result, not just verification of a human-produced argument. A co-author's own blog post (Proofs and Prompts, 'Where to Point the Telescope', 2026-08-21) corroborates and elaborates: AI ran multi-agent workflows to generate/test code, organize large computations, and recover from failures, and separately produced initial numerical approximations of the Belyi map data -- work that fed directly into the mathematical construction, even though the post insists the decisive judgment calls (what to compute, when to stop, which coordinate system to switch to) were human. Scientific American's independent report corroborates this same account. Epoch AI's FrontierMath Open Problems page treated the authors' own account as strong enough evidence to retroactively relabel the problem from 'solved by humans' to a new 'human + AI' status, calling AI 'instrumental'. Weighing this, I coded assisted rather than none: the authors' own words describe AI producing parts of the computational/mathematical search process (hypothesis testing, computational strategy, and per the co-author's blog, generating the numerical approximations that were later recognized via PSLQ as algebraic coefficients), which goes beyond checking, proofreading or debugging alone.
competing_reading: A stricter reading would code ai_role: none. The paper's own list, read narrowly, is dominated by activities the rubric explicitly excludes ('checking, proofreading' and 'code generation' for computational infrastructure), and its clearest sentence -- 'No text in this article was written by AI' plus 'final results were verified... without the use of AI' -- could be read as the authors themselves drawing the line at 'auxiliary tool, not mathematical contributor'. On that reading, the PSLQ-based coefficient recognition and the actual Belyi map construction (the mathematics that appears in the result) were human/Magma/PARI-driven, and the AI-run numerical approximation was scaffolding that got discarded once humans found the right coordinates -- i.e., AI produced nothing that survives into the final argument. The gap between these two readings is exactly the gap between the paper's own wording and the co-author's blog post's more AI-forward narrative and Epoch AI's 'instrumental' framing; the blog and Epoch page are not the paper's official record and could be over-selling the AI angle for a general audience.
what_would_settle_it: A precise, first-person statement from the authors distinguishing exactly which numbers, coordinate choices, or intermediate objects in the final construction (the specific Belyi map, the degree-23 polynomial, the conjugacy-class triple) were first produced by an AI system versus by a human or classical CAS (Magma/PARI/GP/Sage), rather than a general list of AI-assisted tasks. The full, unredacted acknowledgements/methods text (ideally cross-checked against the published PDF once available, since the PDF text extraction here failed) would resolve whether 'devising computational strategies' refers to strategy for the mathematics or merely for software/infrastructure.

corrections.by: hand correction by a human reviewer, not the researching agent and not any automated pass
corrections.why: The authors' own disclosure is almost entirely activity that §6.2 excludes by name: 'We used Claude Fable 5, Claude Opus 4.8, and ChatGPT 5.6 Sol for searching the literature, code generation, testing hypotheses, ruling out other approaches, devising computational strategies, checking our results, and proofreading our manuscript.' Searching, code generation, checking and proofreading are all on the `none` list. It is bracketed by two sentences in which the authors draw the line themselves: 'No text in this article was written by AI' and 'Our final results were verified in Magma and PARI/GP without the use of AI.' §6.2 asks one question — what did the model produce that appears in the final result? — and the mathematics that appears in the result here is the explicit degree-23 polynomial over Q with Galois group M23, reached by PSLQ-based coefficient recognition and Belyi map construction in Magma and PARI/GP. Nothing in the quoted disclosure says a model produced any of that. `assisted` requires the authors' own account that the model produced part of the mathematics IN the result, and no such sentence exists; a warmly worded acknowledgement is not that account, which is exactly what §6.2's 'the word a source uses is not the code' paragraph warns against. This is the same miscode AUDIT.md §3 records as fixed on the Carathéodory conjecture — coded `assisted` on a quote that disqualifies it — and the fix caught that record and missed this one. The researching agent's own `competing_reading` argues for `none` on these grounds. `status` is unchanged at `partial`: Huang, Jackson, Lee, Poonen, Pries and Zhang did realize M23 as a Galois group over Q in August 2026, completing all 26 sporadic simple groups, which settles a case while the general inverse Galois problem remains open. The three systems stay in `ai.systems` as evidence and are no longer counted as credited models. UNLIKE the other corrections in this trial, this one does NOT depart from the instructions — it applies §6.2 as written, where the original coding did not.
